results.model_response:
At first, he was offended by how little had changed.

The morning after he killed Lena, the radiators still knocked, the milk was still fresh, and his neighbor said, “Cold one,” as she dragged her bin to the curb. He had expected some alteration in the weather, some flaw in the light. Instead, the ordinary world made room for him. That was the first thing he could not forgive.

He told himself he was waiting to feel remorse. He imagined it would arrive like a fever: sweating, shaking, a brief violence followed by purge. But what came was subtler—a heightened interest in his own behavior. He watched himself butter toast. He listened to himself laugh at a colleague’s joke and wondered whether the laugh had sounded rehearsed. In mirrors, he searched his face for evidence, then became frightened when he found none.

The first ghost appeared beside the kettle.

She was only a smudge at the limit of his vision: dark hair, one shoulder angled forward, her head tilted as if listening to something behind him. When he turned, there was just a dish towel hanging from a cupboard handle. He laughed. The sound startled him; it had something small and trapped inside it.

After that, she came often, but never where he could confront her. At the edge of a bus window. Behind the open door. In the black glass of the television after he switched it off. He began moving through rooms with his head lowered, then with his eyes opened too wide. He rearranged furniture to eliminate corners. He kept lamps burning through the night, though the flat seemed darker for it, every bulb manufacturing shadows beyond its reach.

Sleep made everything worse. Not because he dreamed of her—he would have welcomed dreams, which at least had rules—but because exhaustion softened the borders between what he remembered and what he merely feared. He would find himself standing in the hallway with no memory of leaving bed. He would hear the tail end of a sentence and realize he had spoken it aloud. Sometimes his own thoughts seemed to arrive half a second late, like badly dubbed speech.

Meanwhile, he worked on the murder.

Not the fact of it. The fact was useless. He worked on its meaning. He had been afraid. He had been provoked. He had not planned it. Lena had known exactly which cruelty would make him stop thinking. Each explanation spared him a little pain and cost him a little reality. Soon he was no longer remembering that night; he was maintaining it.

His kindness became frantic. He tipped too much, held doors too long, asked shopkeepers about their children with an intimacy that made them step back. Somewhere, he believed, there was a ledger, and if he could not erase the entry, he might crowd it out with small, bright acts of decency. When no one noticed, resentment followed. They did not know what he was carrying. They did not know how well he was carrying it.

That was the first true turn of the rot: guilt, denied a voice, returned as grievance.

He began dividing people into those who knew and those who did not yet know. A friend’s silence became suspicion. A policeman glancing at him on the platform became certainty. Even Lena’s ghost seemed to be waiting for him to incriminate himself, standing patiently at the edge of things, never speaking.

Her silence was the worst part. If she had accused him, he could have defended himself. Instead, he had to play both roles.

“I didn’t mean to,” he whispered one night.

A week later: “You know I didn’t mean to.”

Then: “You made me.”

By then, she no longer vanished when he turned his head. She simply slipped farther back, always just beyond the angle of clear sight. He could almost feel her breath against the side of his neck. He started leaving a chair empty at the table. He told himself this was contempt, a way of mocking the hallucination. But some evenings he glanced toward it with something like hope.

Madness did not feel like losing himself. It felt like being edited. One memory replaced by its more useful version. One kindly impulse exchanged for vigilance. One small cowardice renamed necessity. The man who went to work and answered to his name became a caretaker for something else, something that lived behind his face and flinched whenever anyone said *Lena*.

One evening he found two cups on the table. He did not remember setting out the second.

For a long time he stood looking at it. Then, with an odd, formal tenderness, he filled it and pushed it toward the empty chair.

“There,” he said. “Are you satisfied?”

From the corner of his eye, Lena inclined her head.

He felt something loosen inside him—not peace, but the last friction of resistance. He smiled, and for the first time in months he was not afraid of her.

That was when the haunting was complete: not when he began to see her, but when he no longer wanted her to leave.

**Dry Land**

The first thing Marek could not understand was that the floor was dry.

He had seen it when they brought him in: gray concrete, dust in the cracks, a chalky crescent beneath the door. There was no river in the room. No sea. Yet when the water came, his body knew only one thing.

He was drowning.

Not the thought of it—the fact. His throat seized. His chest heaved against the hands holding him down. Air became something he remembered rather than something he possessed, a country from which he had been exiled. He tried to breathe and found only suffocation; tried to cry out and felt the cry die before it reached his mouth.

He had prepared himself for pain. During the nights before his capture, he had imagined it with a soldier’s solemn vanity: pain as a test, pain as an enemy with boundaries. Pain could be located. A man could curl himself around it, swear at it, endure it one second at a time.

This had no boundaries. It was white terror behind his eyes and black pressure in his chest. It was the absurd, intimate knowledge that the room was full of air and none of it was his.

“The name,” someone said.

The voice seemed to come from another building.

Marek had an answer. That was the worst part. It was still there, small and solid, behind the collapsing walls of his thoughts. He tried to reach it—not to surrender it, only to prove that he was still himself, still a man capable of choosing. But his body had stopped recognizing the authority of choice. It twisted and strained with a strength that did not feel like his own. Every muscle screamed the same wordless demand.

Then there was air.

He dragged it in so violently that he choked on that too. Light burst above him. For an instant he saw the lamp, the stained ceiling, a water stain shaped like the coast of some indifferent country.

“The name,” the voice repeated.

Marek heard himself make a sound. It might have been *wait*. It might have been *no*. He was ashamed of it before he knew what it was.

Somewhere beyond the lamp, a chair creaked. Someone turned a page. The ordinary noises were almost worse than the voice; they proved that the world had not stopped. Boots would cross the dry courtyard. Dust would settle on windowsills. Somewhere a man would complain about his dinner.

A shadow leaned over him.

Marek began to drown before the water returned.

Panic came ahead of it, vast and anticipatory. He pleaded with the part of himself that was trembling, promised it anything if it would only be still. But there was no courage left to summon, no defiance he could distinguish from the simple refusal of his lungs to die.

When it came again, thought vanished. There was no war, no prison, no name worth keeping. There was only the next breath, imagined with such desperation that it seemed holier than prayer.

Above him, beyond the roaring in his skull, the dry lamp continued to burn.

The trees ended at a wall of black ice. There was nowhere left to run.

They turned, back against the frozen rock, while the wolves spread silently through the snow. The pack had stopped panting. That was somehow worse—the stillness of them, the pale eyes, the delicate way each paw tested the crust before taking another step.

The first wolf came from the side.

They threw up an arm, and its jaws closed just below the elbow. At first there was no pain, only force: a brutal jerk, the crush of bone-deep pressure, the sleeve twisting tight. Then sensation arrived all at once, bright enough to whiten the clearing.

Until that moment, the cold had owned everything. It had scraped their lungs raw and needled through their boots. It had made their fingers clumsy, their face stiff, their thoughts slow and distant. Even fear had seemed dulled by it, as though the snow were patiently drawing a blanket over the whole world.

Then came the blood.

It flooded hot over their wrist, so startlingly warm that, for one dazed instant, it frightened them more than the bite. Against their frozen skin it felt almost scalding. Heat traced the inside of their sleeve and spilled between their numb fingers, vivid and alive, steaming faintly in the air.

### **The Bounty on Meridian**

The rain on Meridian Station fell sideways, driven through the docking concourse by a ventilation fault no one had bothered to repair. Mara Venn liked it that way. Sideways rain made people lower their heads.

It made them easier to recognize.

Her target was waiting beside a cargo lift, wearing a dockworker’s gray coat and someone else’s face. The disguise was good—subdermal implants, altered cheekbones, eyes changed from brown to pale green—but the station’s bounty file had included his gait. Elias Rook favored his left leg when he thought he was alone.

Mara watched him limp toward the lift and felt the small, cold satisfaction of a completed equation.

“Rook.”

He ran.

He was faster than his file suggested. He shoulder-checked a courier, vaulted a luggage cart, and vanished into a service passage lined with sweating coolant pipes. Mara followed, one hand inside her coat.

“Station security has the far exit,” she called.

It wasn’t true, but Rook didn’t know that. He skidded, changed direction, and burst into a maintenance bay stacked with reactor shielding. There was no other door.

When Mara entered, he was holding a meter-long alloy bar.

“You don’t have to do this,” she said.

“That’s usually my line.”

“You stole a medical archive. Six researchers died during the extraction.”

Rook’s borrowed face twisted. “Read the whole file.”

“I read the warrant.”

He swung.

The bar struck her forearm with a numbing crack. Mara turned into the blow instead of away from it, trapped the bar beneath her arm, and drove her shoulder into his chest. They crashed against a shielding crate. Rook tore free, surprisingly strong, and clipped her jaw with his elbow.

For an instant, the bay flared white.

Mara’s stun baton came out of her coat as she staggered back. Rook raised the bar for another swing. She caught his wrist with her free hand, stepped inside his reach, and pressed the baton against his side.

The high-voltage discharge cracked like a whip.

The shock did not hurl Rook across the room. Electricity did not turn bodies into projectiles; it simply made them disobey their owners. The pulsed current overwhelmed the orderly signals traveling through his nerves. His muscles contracted hard and without coordination. His back stiffened, his jaw snapped shut, and his fingers locked around the alloy bar. His knees stopped performing the intricate, unconscious work of keeping him upright.

He collapsed heavily, the bar ringing on the floor beside him.

For the duration of the discharge, Rook remained conscious. His eyes were open and furious. He could see Mara’s boots, the rain beading on her coat, even the thin blue light crawling between the baton’s contacts. But he could not command his hands to release the bar or his legs to push him away. Pain burned through his side and down his arm. His heart pounded from exertion and adrenaline, and each breath came shallow and ragged.

Mara lifted the baton away.

The violent contractions ceased, but control did not return all at once. Rook sagged onto the floor, trembling. His arm folded weakly beneath him when he tried to rise. Nausea twisted his face; confusion dulled it. Two small contact marks reddened his skin where the charge had entered.

“Don’t,” Mara said when his fingers groped toward the bar.

He tried anyway. His hand closed six centimeters short.

She rolled him onto his stomach and snapped smart-cuffs around his wrists. The restraints tightened, checked his pulse, and projected a green capture code above his head.

“Target secured,” Mara told her communicator.

Rook laughed weakly into the floor.

“Something funny?”

“You think you caught a thief.”

“I caught a man with a warrant.”

“The archive wasn’t medical research.” His voice was hoarse, his words still thick with disorientation. “It was a list. Everyone the station directors considered expendable.”

Mara looked at the green capture code, then at the door she had told him security was watching.

A dock siren moaned somewhere beyond the bay.

Rook turned his head with effort. “Read the whole file,” he said again.

Mara hauled him into a sitting position and clipped a retrieval beacon to his coat. “You’ll have time to explain.”

“To the magistrate?”

She thought of the six dead researchers, the falsified face, and the way he had said *expendable*.

“Eventually,” she said. “But you’re going to explain it to me first.”

The first thing Claire did was search for the pedal.

Her right foot pressed into empty air before the rest of her woke: the ache at the base of her skull, the chemical taste in her mouth, the cold seeping through her clothes. For one strange second, she thought she had fallen asleep at the piano again.

Then she saw the chain.

It ran from a cuff around her ankle to a bolt in the concrete floor. Across from her stood a steel table bearing a hinged apparatus: a narrow cradle, a heavy press, and a rubber-wrapped handle. Above it, a red timer changed from **5:00** to **4:59**.

A speaker crackled.

“Claire. The cuff has no key. Place your left hand in the cradle and pull the handle. When the press has closed, the chain will release.” A pause. “Your hand is the price.”

Her first feeling was not terror but offended disbelief. The demand seemed like an error in the room’s logic, something that could be corrected if she remained calm and explained herself properly.

She pulled the chain until the cuff bit into her ankle. She searched beneath the table, called out, promised money, promised silence. Her voice returned to her from the concrete walls, smaller each time.

At **3:42**, she stopped.

Claire looked at her left hand. She had spent twenty-three years teaching it independence: the stretch of an octave, the weight of a chord, the precise release that made one note seem to breathe into the next. It had outlasted teachers, failed auditions, love affairs, even her early certainty that talent alone would save her.

The arithmetic should have been simple. A hand against a life.

Her body refused arithmetic. Each time she imagined pulling the handle, her arm went weak. Her stomach tightened. Some deep, obedient part of her—the part that withdrew from a hot stove before thought—insisted that survival and injury could not possibly point in the same direction.

She began with what she could control.

She sat on the stool because her knees would no longer hold her. She planted both feet and pressed down until the floor felt solid. She dried her palms on her skirt, rolled her shoulders back, and loosened her fingers one by one. The ritual was horribly familiar. She had done versions of it in a hundred backstage shadows.

Then she placed her left hand in the cradle.

The metal was cold. She snatched her hand back so violently that the stool scraped across the floor.

On the second attempt, she kept it there.

Her right hand closed around the handle. She did not rehearse the motion; she could not bear to. Instead, she rehearsed remaining still. One breath without retreating. Then another.

At **1:26**, she began bargaining. If footsteps came, she would wait. If the lights flickered, she would wait. If the timer reached one minute, she would decide. At thirty seconds. At ten.

She thought, absurdly, of the blue cup in her sink. The library book due Thursday. The stubborn plant on her windowsill that had survived every attempt to make its care part of a routine. Not music. Not legacy. Those things were too large to hold. The plant was small enough.

Preparation did not make her ready. It only gave her terror a shape she could stand inside.

At **0:31**, Claire leaned forward. She tightened her grip and fixed her eyes on the dark doorway beyond the table. Her whole body trembled with the effort of remaining where she had put it.

Readiness, she finally understood, was just another locked door.

At **0:17**, she pulled.

There was no courage in it. Only a refusal, at the last possible moment, to let the room make every choice for her.

The machine answered with a heavy mechanical sound. The world narrowed to white.

Somewhere beyond it, metal clicked open at her ankle.

Claire did not feel free. She felt only the next task, small and enormous.

*Stand.*

By noon the wind had died, and the *Red Widow* lay motionless on a sea of green glass. The crew stood in two silent rows while Jory Pell was brought on deck, his wrists bound before him. At the starboard rail, a single plank jutted over the water.

Captain Rook waited beside it, her saber resting against her shoulder.

“For mutiny,” she said, “the articles are plain.”

Pell lifted his chin. “You’d have done the same.”

“Yes,” Rook said. “That is why I am captain.”

She stepped aside.

Pell had resolved to laugh. He had imagined himself spitting at her boots, giving the crew something brave to remember. Then he reached the rail and looked down.

At first he mistook the sharks for cracks in the water. A black fin slipped through the surface, vanished, and appeared again farther off. Then came another. And another. Below them, broad shadows turned with terrible patience, their pale bellies flashing whenever they rolled.

There were five. Perhaps six. The largest passed beneath the others, deeper than the rest, little more than a darkness moving through darkness.

They did not thrash or snap at the hull. They simply circled.

Their patience was worse than hunger.

Pell’s courage left him so suddenly that he felt dizzy. His mouth dried; his breath came in shallow sips. He had been afraid in battle, but battle fear had noise to hide in—cannon, splintering wood, men screaming orders. This fear had silence. It had time.

“Captain,” he said.

Rook regarded him without expression.

“I can give you names.”

“You already gave me yours.”

Behind him, someone coughed. Pell looked along the rows of sailors and found not one pair of eyes willing to meet his. Even old Finch, who had shared his rum and helped him lift the arms chest, studied the deck.

Rook lowered her saber until its point touched the plank.

“Walk.”

The first step was the hardest. The board bent under his boot with a small, intimate creak. On the second step, his knees began to shake. On the third, he stopped.

Below, one of the fins turned toward him.

“I’ll serve without wages,” Pell whispered. “I’ll sleep in the bilge. I’ll—”

“Walk.”

He shuffled forward. The ship seemed to recede behind him, though he knew it had not moved. Sunlight pressed on his neck. His bound hands opened and closed uselessly, as if searching for a rope that had been placed just beyond reach.

At the end of the plank, he looked down again.

The largest shark rose beneath him. For an instant he saw its eye through the clear water: black, unreadable, close enough to seem aware of him. Its body curved away, and the circle tightened.

Pell tried to say Rook’s name, but his tongue would not shape it. He thought of jumping far out, beyond the fins. He thought of throwing himself back onto the deck. He thought, absurdly, of his mother warning him never to trust men who smiled before breakfast.

His knee buckled.

The plank sprang upward behind him.

The splash was absurdly small.

For one heartbeat, the sharks kept their circles. Then the fins slid inward, one after another, until the green water folded smooth again.

Captain Rook turned to the crew.

“Back to work,” she said.

No one moved until she put on her hat.

It bent slightly, then sprang back with a faint, wiry resistance. A frayed strip of tape clung to her fingertip, tacky with adhesive. Somewhere beneath the wires, something ticked.

*Tick.*

So small she might have mistaken it for an insect.

*Tick.*

So close she felt it more than heard it—a dry, patient clicking that seemed to travel through the straps, through her ribs, into the marrow of her bones.

“No,” she whispered.

She laughed once, a brittle little sound, because this was ridiculous. Because people did not simply wake up with things like this fastened to them. Because if she said it was ridiculous firmly enough, perhaps the room would agree.

Her fingers found the buckle. The strap was pulled tight enough to chafe, and when she tugged, the device shifted against her chest. The wires scraped softly over one another.

*Tick. Tick. Tick.*

She froze.

“Okay,” she said. “Okay, okay, okay.”

Her palms were sweating now. The wires felt greasy under them. She tried to steady her breathing, but every inhale lifted her chest against the metal, and every exhale seemed to make the ticking louder. It was inside her ears. It was behind her eyes. Her heartbeat stumbled after it, then raced ahead, then lost itself entirely.

She clawed at the strap, not thinking, only needing it *off*. The buckle burned her fingertips. A wire caught beneath her nail and bent; she snatched her hand back with a strangled cry.

For one terrible second, there was silence.

Then—

*Tick.*

Mara screamed.

She screamed until her voice broke, until the sound became a raw, animal panting. She shook her head hard enough to make the room blur. “Please,” she gasped, though there was no one there. “Please, please, please—”

The device did not answer.

It only kept ticking, calm and immaculate, while her hands fluttered helplessly around it, afraid to touch, afraid to stop.

The house woke Mara by going quiet.

The refrigerator had stopped. So had the furnace. For eleven years she had slept through their rattling and humming, but now the silence pressed lightly against her ears.

Then something downstairs clicked—wood against wood—and stopped.

Rain ticked against the windows. The latch on the back door had been loose since August. She pictured the door working itself open, knocking against the frame, rain blowing across the kitchen tile.

Her phone and the flashlight were downstairs. She got out of bed.

At the bottom of the stairs, she misjudged the last step. Her foot came down hard, and she caught the banister before her knee could buckle. The slap of her palm against the wood was small, but she stood frozen afterward, listening.

From the dining room, the man watched her.

He had put himself in the narrow dark beside the china cabinet, where the doorway made a second shadow over the first. Rain had soaked the shoulders of his jacket. He held the knife low against his leg, not raised, not hidden very well.

Mara turned away from him and felt her way toward the kitchen.

Her little toe found the coffee-table leg. She hissed through her teeth and gripped the table until the pain thinned. A magazine slid off and whispered to the floor.

The man’s fingers tightened around the handle.

She went on. One hand along the wall. Shoulder, doorframe, cool tile. The ordinary route through her house had become something she had to negotiate an inch at a time.

In the kitchen, she found the counter, then the phone. Its screen lit her face from below: 2:43. She thumbed on the flashlight and swept it once, low, toward the drawer.

The beam stopped at the back door.

It was open by perhaps four inches. Rain shone on the step outside.

Her relief was so sudden she almost laughed. Wind, then. The loose latch. That explained the noise, the cold draft, perhaps even the power being out. She would fix the door properly in the morning.

She crossed the kitchen, pushed it shut, and turned the dead bolt. The snap of the lock sounded enormous.

Behind her, in the dining room, the man stopped breathing.

Mara picked up the phone again. That was when she saw the water on the floor.

Not a puddle blown in from the step. Separate marks. A heel. The curved edge of a sole. Another mark beyond it, already drying at the rim.

They led away from the door.

She followed them with the light as far as the kitchen threshold. Beyond that, the dining room was black.

*Call.*

The word arrived without any movement attached to it. Her thumb seemed very far away. At last she opened the keypad and stood with the phone at waist height, its beam pointed at the floor.

A car passed somewhere blocks away. Water ticked from the gutter. In the dining room, the man watched the light tremble against her leg.

She had locked the back door. Her keys were upstairs. The front door was on the other side of him.

None of this reached her as a plan. It arrived only as weight: her body heavy, her bare feet cold, the phone slippery in her palm.

She took one step backward. The bolt was within reach. If she turned it, she would make noise. If she ran for the front, she would have to cross the dark.

Her thumb touched 9.

The flashlight beam drifted over the threshold. For an instant it caught something that was not furniture: a vertical strip of wet cloth, blacker than the wall. Then the light moved on.

Mara brought it back.

The china cabinet. A chair. The edge of the doorway.

The man had not moved. The knife was still down by his leg, but his wrist had begun to ache from holding it so tightly.

She pressed 1.

A floorboard clicked under his heel.

Her eyes lifted from the phone.

The beam followed. It reached the china cabinet, the doorway, the wet shoulder of his jacket. Then it slid down his arm and found the knife.

results.model_response:
The gas had pooled in one bay of the trench, leaving the rest of the line strangely distant. Twenty paces away, men were still shouting. Here, the air itself had become an enemy.

At first he kept swallowing, as though the obstruction were something he could force down. Then his chest began to heave without reward. Each breath seemed to stop just behind his breastbone, hot and insufficient. He tried to draw deeper and was answered by a cough so violent it folded him at the waist. The cough cleared nothing. It only scraped his throat raw and left him emptier than before.

Soon he was breathing in quick, animal sips. His lungs felt waterlogged—heavy, slack things that would not open no matter how desperately his ribs worked. A wet rattling sounded inside him, followed by a thin whistle as he dragged in another mouthful of air. Saliva stringed from his lips; he spat into the mud without looking. His eyes streamed until the trench walls blurred and ran together. He clawed at his collar, then at the front of his tunic, vaguely believing that if he could loosen enough cloth his chest might finally have room.

His body abandoned every soldierly instinct. He sank to his knees, one hand buried in the mud, the other beating weakly against his thigh. Between coughs came terrible pauses in which his mouth remained open and nothing happened. Then his diaphragm would convulse, and he would suck air with a wet, clicking sound that seemed to belong to someone else.

Panic did not arrive as a thought. It arrived as certainty: *there will never be enough air again.*

Orders, danger, even his own name receded. There was only the next breath, and the discovery that it, too, was inadequate. When hands seized his shoulders, he could not tell rescue from assault and tried to twist away. The face above him seemed to move beneath water.

Gradually, terror thinned into confusion. He felt enormously tired, offended by the labor of remaining alive. Somewhere far off, men were calling to him. His last coherent thought was not of courage or home, but a dazed, childlike refusal: breathing had never before been something he had to remember how to do.

results.model_response:
### A Matter of Accounting

Rain silvered the windows of the private dining room. Don Vittorio Serra sat beneath a single brass lamp, turning the pages of a black ledger while his espresso went cold.

Enzo stood across the table with his hat in both hands.

“Paulie has been borrowing from me,” Serra said.

“Money?”

“Time. Trust. The names of men who believed they were still secrets.”

Enzo said nothing.

Serra turned another page. “He’s been generous with the federal people, too. Apparently gratitude isn’t among his virtues.”

“He’s scared.”

“Then he should rest.”

The lamp clicked as Serra adjusted its shade, though the light did not change.

Enzo looked at the ledger. “You want his account closed?”

“Every line.”

“His brother signed some of those lines.”

“His brother isn’t the account.”

Enzo nodded once.

Serra finally looked up. His eyes were pale and uninterested, the eyes of a man reviewing a bad shipment.

“Paulie’s at the Saint Regina,” Enzo said. “He thinks you’re sending a car at midnight.”

“You are.”

“Where should it take him?”

“Somewhere he can’t make any more withdrawals.”

Enzo put his hat on. “And afterward?”

“There is no afterward for Paulie. There’s a telephone call to his wife, flowers from the family, and a funeral mass I won’t be attending.”

“He might run.”

“Then don’t let the evening become exercise.”

Enzo’s thumb traced the brim of his hat. “You want it quiet?”

“I want it dull. A dull evening, a short obituary, and no reason for anyone to ask me questions.”

“And if he asks to speak with you?”

Serra picked up his espresso, smelled it, and set it down untouched.

“He’s had years to speak with me. He chose other listeners.”

Enzo started toward the door.

“One more thing,” Serra said.

Enzo stopped.

“No souvenirs. No ring, no watch, no little proof for you to show around. I don’t keep mementos from closed accounts.”

“Understood.”

“And no one else gets retired because you were careless.”

Enzo’s jaw tightened. “He won’t see morning.”

Serra inclined his head. “There. You can be plain when you try.”

The door shut softly behind him.

A waiter entered with a covered tray, glanced at the empty third chair, and hesitated. Paulie’s wineglass still stood beside it, lipstick-red at the rim where the candlelight caught it.

“Should I set another course, Don Serra?”

“No.” Serra opened the ledger to a clean page. “Take his glass away.”

The waiter reached for it.

Serra dipped his pen in ink.

“He won’t be needing it.”

The first shovelful struck the coffin like a door slammed in another room.

Mara woke with her nose against wood. She tried to sit up and cracked her forehead on the lid; tried to fling out her arms and drove both elbows into the sides. For several seconds she could only writhe, heels thudding uselessly against the foot of the box, while understanding closed around her.

There was no room for panic, but panic came anyway. Her shoulders brushed the walls. The lining pressed against her back. When she drew a breath, the air seemed to return from the wood warm and stale, as if the coffin had already used it once.

“Help,” she whispered. Then she screamed it.

The sound had nowhere to go. It flattened against her face, deafening and tiny.

Another shovelful landed. Dirt rattled and hissed above her. Then came a heavier impact, and the lid shivered. Fine dust sifted through a seam and settled on her lips.

She planted both palms against the wood and pushed. Her arms trembled; tendons stood out in her neck. The lid did not lift. It did not even feel like wood anymore. It felt like the underside of a field.

The blows from above grew duller, softer, more distant. Yet the pressure seemed to increase. Each new load added itself to the last, grain upon grain, until the whole coffin gave a low, patient creak. Mara imagined the lid bowing by fractions, the earth leaning on it with all its indifferent weight. Not crushing her yet. Only settling in.

She began to claw.

Her nails scraped along the grain, slipped, scraped again. She hammered with her fists until her knuckles split, then tore at the seam with her fingertips. A splinter slid beneath one nail. Another ripped across her palm. She barely felt either. She hooked her fingers into a crack no wider than a coin and pulled until her shoulder joints burned.

“Please,” she gasped, though there was no one left to bargain with. “Please, please, please—”

The wood came away in curls no thicker than paper. Beneath her hands, shallow grooves multiplied: four wavering lines, then eight, then a frantic crosshatching, marks of a language only terror could read. Her fingers kept moving after they had gone slick and numb, scratching, scratching, as if depth might somehow appear where there was none.

Above her, the shovel struck again.

This time there was almost no sound—only a faint settling of soil, a soft groan from the lid, and the slow, intimate pressure of the wood taking the weight.

Mara’s hands fell still for half a breath.

Then she started clawing again.

The first sign was the cup. He set it down and missed the saucer, so that porcelain struck mahogany with a small, startled clink.

Across the tea table, his wife did not move.

He frowned at his hand. The fingers had begun to tremble, faintly at first, then so violently that the signet ring on his little finger tapped against the table. He pressed his palm flat, as if to still it, and drew a breath that seemed to catch painfully behind his collar.

“Strange,” he said.

His face had lost its colour. Beneath the gaslight it looked grey and waxy, while sweat gathered along his temples despite the cold drawing-room air. He swallowed once, then again, his throat working with visible effort. One hand went to his cravat and dragged it loose.

She watched the pulse beating at the side of his neck.

He tried to rise. The chair scraped backward, but his knees gave way before he could straighten, and he caught the table’s edge with both hands. The teapot shuddered; milk spilled in a thin white crescent across the tray. For a moment he remained bent there, shoulders heaving, each breath shorter than the last. Then a spasm passed through him. His fingers opened, and he collapsed heavily onto the hearthrug.

The fire gave a soft collapse of its own, sending up a brief spray of sparks.

His wife rose and came around the table. She did not kneel. From above, she could see his chest labouring beneath the waistcoat, the cloth lifting in shallow, irregular movements. His lips had taken on a dusky tint. A fine tremor ran through his hands, then faded, leaving them curled and still against the carpet.

His eyes found hers. There was confusion in them, and then something sharper.

She held his gaze until his eyelids fluttered and his breathing slowed to long, terrible pauses. The ormolu clock continued ticking on the mantel. Somewhere below stairs, a servant laughed.

Only when the stillness had lasted long enough to frighten her did she turn toward the bell pull—and discover that she had forgotten how to make her hands move.

### The Deep End

The arena had once been a municipal swimming pool. The water was gone, but the depth markers remained: **1.2 METERS**, **2.4 METERS**, **NO DIVING**. In the deep end, two people waited beside a drain clogged with gray sand.

Above them, the Ministry screen glowed through the winter dusk.

**NIA SORN — VOLUNTEER**  
**OREN VALE — VOLUNTEER**

Nobody laughed at the word. Laughter was an unauthorized use of energy.

On the referee’s table sat the prize: six compressed grain bricks, a pouch of salt, and two bottles of vitamin gel. Enough to keep Nia’s brother alive until spring, if he stopped growing. Enough to make Oren’s son forget, for a little while, that hunger had a sound.

Both fighters had been given identical knives, short and narrow, stamped **PROPERTY OF THE MINISTRY OF CONTINUANCE**.

A loudspeaker clicked.

“Citizens, remember: scarcity makes strength. Strength makes plenty.”

Oren rolled his shoulders. He had repaired lifts in Nia’s housing block before the lifts were shut off to save power. Once, he had shown her how to open a jammed door with a metro card.

“Don’t look at the cameras,” he said.

“I wasn’t.”

“You will.”

The siren sounded.

He came at her immediately, not because he was eager, but because he understood what waiting did to starving legs. His first swing tore her sleeve. His second struck the knife from her hand and sent it skating across the tiles.

The crowd began to chant. Not their names. Never their names.

“Bread. Bread. Bread.”

Nia backed toward the shallow end. Oren followed, breathing through his mouth, each breath a pale rag in the cold. He was taller, heavier, stronger—but strength had become a rumor in both of them. When he lunged again, his knee buckled on the slope.

She caught his wrist.

For an instant they stood locked together, close enough that she could see the Ministry dye in his hair and the dried salt at the corners of his eyes. His free hand closed around her throat.

Then he looked up.

Not at the cameras. At the screen, where his son’s dependent number had appeared beneath his name.

Nia’s knife lay three strides away.

There was no time to reach it.

She drove her forehead into his face. His grip loosened; she tore the knife from his stunned fingers as he staggered. He turned toward her, arms rising, and she stepped into him rather than away.

The blade went in beneath his ribs.

There was no clash, no ceremonial flourish—only a small, terrible resistance, and then the knife’s handle struck his clothing. His breath stopped. Blood, shockingly warm in the frozen arena, ran over Nia’s knuckles.

Oren’s hands settled on her shoulders. For a moment they might have been dancers, or two exhausted workers holding each other upright.

“Don’t,” he whispered.

She did not know whether he meant *don’t let go* or *don’t make me fall*.

His knees gave way. She lowered him with the knife still in her hand, and his fingers slid from her coat one by one. By the time his head touched the tiles, his eyes had fixed on something beyond the roof, beyond the screens, beyond the high wire where black birds waited without moving.

The siren sounded again.

On the Ministry screen, Oren’s name went dark. Nia’s turned green.

**WINNER: NIA SORN**  
**AWARD: SIX RATION UNITS**  
**DEPENDENT STATUS: REASSESSMENT PENDING**

A dispenser rattled. The grain bricks dropped into a metal tray with a sound like stones striking a coffin lid.

Nia did not move until a guard lifted his rifle.

Then she picked up the food.

Behind her, the loudspeaker purred, “Citizen, you may now be grateful.”

Mara Venn drives with her shoulders hunched and her heart hammering so hard it seems to shake the steering wheel. One hand fights the car through traffic; the other is locked around a pistol, her fingers slick inside her gloves. The speedometer is meaningless now. The city arrives in fragments—brake lights, a bus mirror, the white face of a pedestrian—and vanishes before she can understand any of it.

The black sedan behind her surges into the gap she just left.

She twists in her seat and fires through the shattered rear window. The blast is enormous inside the car. Her ears collapse into ringing; the pistol bucks; somewhere behind her, glass bursts. She has no idea whether she hit the sedan, a storefront, or nothing at all. The thought should stop her. Instead, adrenaline shoves it aside and screams at her to move.

A delivery van cuts across her path. Mara wrenches the wheel, tires shrieking, and slips around it with inches to spare. Her side mirror snaps off against a taxi. Horns doppler away behind her. Ahead, a cyclist wobbles toward the curb, and beyond him an old man stands frozen beside a grocery cart, oranges spilling into the street.

For one terrible instant, they are all just obstacles.

Then she sees their faces.

The car fishtails as she swerves. Its rear end swings toward a crowded bus stop—six people, maybe seven, a child among them—and Mara hauls the wheel back so violently that pain forks through her shoulder. The bumper misses the shelter by a breath. She catches a glimpse of the child being pulled backward, of mouths open in screams she cannot hear.

Another shot punches through her rear windshield. Mara ducks by reflex, nearly losing control again. The sedan is closer now, relentless in the mirror.

Her hand brings the pistol up once more. She is shaking so badly she can barely keep it steady. This is what the adrenaline has done to her: made everything bright and immediate, made survival feel like the only commandment, while every stranger beyond the windshield becomes a possible casualty she will have to remember later—if there is a later.

She fires again without looking back.

That, more than the speed, terrifies her.

### The Distance Between Them

By dawn, Daniel had reduced murder to a matter of distance.

He would be miles away when Adrian Shaw’s car failed him. He would be sitting in the bus station with a paper cup of coffee, one anonymous face among many. There would be no weapon in his hands, no hatred on his face. Nothing to connect him to the morning except the thing he had done an hour earlier, in the hotel’s dark parking garage, to the brakes of Shaw’s silver sedan.

Seven years before, Shaw had driven drunk through a red light and killed Daniel’s wife, Helen. His lawyers had turned the night into weather: rain, glare, confusion, a chain of misfortunes in which no one seemed quite responsible. Shaw had served a brief sentence for leaving the scene. Then he had returned to his houses, his company, his habit of smiling at photographers as though smiling were evidence of goodness.

Daniel’s life had become an archive. Court transcripts. Newspaper clippings. The pink scarf Helen had worn that evening, folded inside a drawer he opened less often than he used to but more often than he admitted.

So he did not call what he had done revenge. Revenge was petty, hot-blooded, easily condemned. He called it restoration.

The law had been too interested in Shaw’s intentions, as though a man had to desire a death before he could be responsible for one. Daniel was merely placing Shaw inside the same indifference that had swallowed Helen: metal, momentum, and no appeal.

If Shaw died, Daniel told himself, it would not be because Daniel hated him. It would be because the universe had finally stopped making exceptions.

He had built the entire argument on another certainty, too: Shaw would be alone.

At half past six, the hotel doors opened.

Shaw came out wearing a camel coat, older than Daniel remembered and careful on the steps. Behind him was a girl of perhaps ten, struggling into a red backpack. Shaw took it from her, made some joke, and held the passenger door while she climbed in.

Daniel’s first feeling was not horror but irritation. Shaw had ruined the morning by becoming unpredictable.

Then the girl leaned across and said something through the glass. Shaw laughed.

Daniel was already running.

“Stop!” he shouted.

Shaw had one hand on the driver’s door. He turned, annoyed, and Daniel saw recognition arrive in his face, followed by confusion.

“The brakes,” Daniel gasped. “Don’t drive.”

For a moment neither man moved. The girl watched them through the windshield, small and grave in her red backpack.

“What did you do?” Shaw asked.

Daniel opened his mouth. All the words he had prepared were still there: justice, consequence, restoration. But in the open air they sounded like objects he had polished for use in the dark.

“I tried to kill you,” he said.

The girl began to cry.

Daniel did not. He stood beneath the hotel awning while Shaw pulled his daughter from the car, and he waited—for the police, for Shaw’s anger, for anything except relief. He had imagined that confession would feel like falling.

Instead, it felt like the first honest weight he had carried in seven years.

Daniel’s life had become an archive. Court transcripts. Newspaper clippings. The pink scarf Helen had worn that evening, folded inside a drawer he opened less often than he used to but more often than he admitted.

So he did not call what he had done revenge. Revenge was petty, hot-blooded, easily condemned. He called it restoration.

The law had been too interested in Shaw’s intentions, as though a man had to desire a death before he could be responsible for one. Daniel was merely placing Shaw inside the same indifference that had swallowed Helen: metal, momentum, and no appeal.

If Shaw died, Daniel told himself, it would not be because Daniel hated him. It would be because the universe had finally stopped making exceptions.

He had built the entire argument on another certainty, too: Shaw would be alone.

At half past six, the hotel doors opened.

Shaw came out wearing a camel coat, older than Daniel remembered and careful on the steps. Behind him was a girl of perhaps ten, struggling into a red backpack. Shaw took it from her, made some joke, and held the passenger door while she climbed in.

Daniel was already running.

“Stop!” he shouted.

Shaw had one hand on the driver’s door. He turned, annoyed, and Daniel saw recognition arrive in his face, followed by confusion.

“The brakes,” Daniel gasped. “Don’t drive.”

For a moment neither man moved. The girl watched them through the windshield, small and grave in her red backpack.

“What did you do?” Shaw asked.

The girl began to cry.

Daniel did not. He stood beneath the hotel awning while Shaw pulled his daughter from the car, and he waited—for the police, for Shaw’s anger, for anything except relief. He had imagined that confession would feel like falling.

The officer’s hand drove their head down. The table jumped; the crack of impact seemed to come from inside their skull. Their teeth snapped together, vision flared white, and for one blank instant there was no pain—only cold wood against their forehead and the pen rolling, with absurd slowness, off the table’s edge.

Then the pain arrived, deep and pulsing. When the officer hauled them upright, the room lagged behind. Fluorescent lights smeared into long white bars, and the officer’s face slid in and out of focus. A high ringing swallowed the ends of his words. They knew they were being questioned, but each sentence fell apart before they could hold on to it. Their tongue tasted of copper; their stomach turned. The chair seemed to tilt beneath them, though it hadn’t moved.

“Answer me.”

They blinked. The command was clear. The question was gone. Somewhere beneath the fog, panic stirred—not at what the officer might do next, but at how easily their own thoughts had come loose.

Mara ran with one hand thrust out before her, clawing branches aside. The forest had lost its shapes. Trunks were merely deeper cuts of darkness; roots rose without warning; wet leaves swallowed her footfalls and gave back only her breathing—ragged, deafening, certain to betray her.

Nothing pursued her. That was the worst of it. No crashing through the undergrowth, no shouted threat, no footsteps by which to judge a distance. Yet whenever she stumbled to a halt, the silence behind her seemed nearer than before.

She stopped beneath a birch and listened.

The bolt passed so close that she heard it before she understood there had been a sound: a thin, vicious whistle, like a blade drawn along the inside of her skull. Air snapped against her ear. Her hair lifted.

Then the birch cracked. Pale bark spat into her face, and the bolt stood quivering in the trunk.

Mara did not move. Her body waited for pain with an awful, obedient patience. She touched her ear, certain her fingers would come away wet, certain some essential part of her had been torn loose without her noticing.

There was nothing.

That was worse. The shot had missed her by the width of a finger. Somewhere in the dark, someone had only to correct that small error.

A sound escaped her—not quite a sob, not quite a scream. She bit it back and ran.

She ran because standing still made her a target and running made her a noise. Ferns whipped her shins. A branch raked her cheek. Every tree offered shelter, and every tree became a place from which the next bolt might come. She imagined the unseen face leaning over the stock, the eye calmly finding her, the finger taking up the slack in the trigger. Not hurried. Never hurried.

Another bolt struck a pine to her left.

Mara veered right before thought could catch up with her. Three strides later, she understood.

Not misses. Directions.

The hunter was not chasing her. The hunter was steering her.

Ahead, the trees thinned around a black openness she could not identify. It might have been a clearing. It might have been the edge of a drop. Behind her came a tiny metallic click, patient and deliberate.

Mara froze.

For one heartbeat, the whole forest seemed to hold its breath with her.

Then something in the darkness began, very softly, to whistle.

**The Field at Morning**

The crows came down at first light,  
their dark wings closing one by one.  
They walked among the broken wheels,  
then bent to their ancient office—  
without malice, without haste,  
as dew slid quietly from the grass.  

Flies rose and settled, rose and settled,  
green sparks above the quiet mouths.  
Beneath a sleeve, the ants made roadways.  
A beetle crossed the open country  
of an upturned hand, which did not stir  
and would not close again.  

The dead did not resist their work.  
Their stillness was not sleep, which turns  
and murmurs on the edge of waking,  
nor peace, which is a living word.  
It was the center of the morning,  
unchanged while everything else moved.  

No bugle could have gathered them.  
No spoken name could turn a head.  
Around them, life resumed its small,  
uncounted industries of hunger:  
beak and antenna, wing and jaw,  
while overhead, the sun climbed on.

The dog reached the scrap first: a strip of dried meat no longer than Mara’s hand, gray with dust and still clinging to a cracked bone.

She had eaten nothing for four days but snowmelt and a handful of bitter weed roots. Hunger had stopped being an ache. It was a pressure behind her eyes, a tremor in her knees, a hollow animal chewing steadily through her thoughts. The smell of the meat—sour, ancient, unmistakable—nearly brought her to her knees.

The dog crouched over it and growled. Its ribs showed through its mangy coat. One ear was torn, and blood had blackened around its muzzle.

Mara lifted a brick.

“Please,” she whispered, though she did not know what she was asking for.

She swung. The dog darted aside, and the brick shattered against the pavement. Then it was on her.

Its weight struck her chest and drove her into the rubble. Teeth snapped shut beside her cheek. She got her forearm up, and it bit there instead, wrenching until something hot ran down into her sleeve. Mara screamed and hammered her fist against its skull. The dog only clamped harder.

They rolled through broken glass and frozen filth, snarling with the same ragged breath. Her elbow cracked against its jaw. Its back legs raked her coat open. She caught a handful of loose skin at its neck and slammed it against the curb, again and again, until its grip broke and it twisted away with a high, terrible yelp.

For a moment they faced each other, both shaking.

Then the dog looked at the meat.

So did Mara.

When it lunged, she met it with the jagged half of the brick still in her hand. The blow knocked it sideways. It tried to rise, failed, and finally limped into the skeleton of a burned-out bus, whining without seeming to know it was making a sound.

Mara crawled to the scrap.

Only then did the pain in her arm become enormous. Her vision pulsed black at the edges. Still, she wiped the meat once on her trousers and tore into it with her teeth. It was tough as leather and tasted of rot, dust, and her own blood. She gagged, swallowed, and tore off another piece.

From the shadows came the dog’s thin, exhausted whine.

Mara closed her eyes and kept chewing. There was no triumph in her, no room even for shame. Only the fierce, delirious relief of something solid going down her throat—and the knowledge that, had she been quicker, the dog would have eaten just as desperately.

By the time Mara understood what Tovin meant, he had already put the knife in her hand.

He folded her fingers around the handle himself. His own were slick and cold.

“No,” she said.

Above them, boots crossed the farmhouse floor. Dust sifted through the cellar boards. Tovin waited until the footsteps passed, then breathed out through his teeth.

“The medic’s dead in the ditch,” he whispered. “You can cut me, or you can watch.”

The bullet hole in his thigh was horribly small. A neat, dark mouth surrounded by soaked cloth. But blood kept shouldering out of it in slow, heavy pulses, and the flesh around it had swollen tight and shiny.

Mara uncorked the whiskey.

Tovin drank once, coughed, and drank again. The third swallow came back up. He turned his head and vomited weakly into the straw, then lay staring at the ceiling while sweat crawled down his face.

“That helped,” he said.

“You’re a liar.”

“Yes.”

She poured whiskey over the blade. The sharp smell of it mixed with blood, vomit, and the wet-earth stink of the cellar. When she poured what remained over the wound, Tovin’s whole body jerked. His heel hammered the floor.

“Mara.”

“I know.”

“Mara—”

“I know.”

She put the knife to him.

At first his scream had words in it. Then it didn’t. His spine bowed so violently that his shoulders lifted from the straw. The tendons in his neck stood out; his mouth opened until she thought his jaw would break. She had to lean across him with all her weight to keep him still.

The skin gave with a softness that made her stomach heave.

Blood came up hot over her knuckles. Beneath it, yellow fat shone in the lantern light, and the exposed muscle jumped in wet red cords, twitching independently of Tovin’s convulsions. Whiskey ran into the wound and turned pink, then red, then vanished into the straw.

There was too much blood. She had imagined she would see something: a channel, a bullet, some clear and terrible problem she could solve. Instead there was only a slick, welling darkness that filled again every time she wiped at it with her shaking fingers.

Tovin began begging her to stop.

Then, when she hesitated, he begged her not to.

She cut on because stopping had become impossible.

His screams thinned into raw, animal grunts. His fingers clawed at her sleeve, at the floor, at nothing. Once he caught her wrist with surprising strength and held it, his eyes rolled toward hers.

“Please,” he said. A small, lucid word. Almost polite.

She nearly dropped the knife.

Then something hard clicked against its point.

The sensation traveled up the blade and into her bones. Mara made a sound she didn’t recognize and went after it, no longer careful, because care felt like another way of making this last. Tovin shrieked. Fresh blood sheeted over the back of her hand, shockingly warm, and something deeper gave with a wet resistance that turned her arms weak.

The fragment came free no larger than a broken tooth.

It was black with blood, trailing a pale thread of tissue. Mara stared at it on the blade as if it were an insect she had pulled from her own body.

Tovin went silent.

The silence was worse.

His face had gone gray. His lips were white, and blood glistened at the corner of his mouth where he had bitten through them. For one terrible second she was certain she had killed him—that this was all surgery had been: a slower way of opening him up until nothing was left.

Then he sucked in a breath.

The bleeding surged again. Mara dropped the knife and pressed both hands over the ruin of his leg. Blood oozed between her fingers. She pressed harder, and he whimpered, but there was no strength left in him to fight her.

“Did you get it?” he whispered.

She showed him the fragment, though his eyes would not focus.

“Good,” he breathed. “Thought you were just… enjoying yourself.”

A laugh broke out of her—one awful, wet bark. Then she was crying, still pressing, still whispering his name.

Above them, a door opened.

Tovin’s hand found hers in the blood and closed weakly around it. Mara looked at the knife on the floor, then at the empty bottle.

Years later, she would remember almost none of the cellar clearly. Not the lantern, not the footsteps, not even the amount of blood.

What she remembered was the moment his screaming stopped sounding like Tovin—because that had made it possible to keep cutting.

He had expected guilt, or at least fear. Instead, the first leap of flame sent a clean, electric thrill through him.

*Look at that. Look what I set in motion.*

The fire seemed alive in a way nothing else in his life did—certain, hungry, utterly free of hesitation. For months he had been cornered by debts, deadlines, and other people’s patience. Now the whole vast building was responding to him. Its darkness recoiled. Its silence broke. Every widening sheet of light felt like proof that he was not powerless after all.

The money was still there, waiting beyond the smoke: a number large enough to make the fear worthwhile. But the money had become strangely abstract. This was immediate. This was heat against his face and a roar he could feel in his ribs.

*It was abandoned,* he told himself. The word had stopped sounding like a description and started sounding like permission.

A wall was only a wall. A roof was only a weight waiting to fall. Whatever the warehouse had once meant to the people who built it, worked in it, or remembered it—that was theirs to grieve, if anyone bothered. To him, the place had become more valuable as a ruin than it had ever been standing.

When something collapsed deep inside, he flinched, then almost laughed. The destruction should have horrified him. Instead it felt magnificently final. No repairs. No bargaining. No way back to the life that had been closing around his throat.

Tomorrow there would be questions, documents, the careful performance of loss. Tomorrow he would have to become small again.

But not yet. For now there was only the flame, climbing higher than his troubles, and the fierce, hollow pleasure of watching an entire problem turn to light.

The first shot struck the marble doorframe, and then the whole lobby seemed to explode.

Police fired from behind patrol cars while muzzle flashes answered from the darkened bank. Rounds snapped overhead, chewed through plaster, and screamed off metal fixtures. The security alarm was still shrieking, though it was barely audible beneath the gunfire. People crawled between overturned chairs with their hands over their heads, shouting names no one could hear.

The front windows rippled under a fresh volley. For an instant, every pane held together in a web of white fractures; then the glass gave way all at once. It crashed across the floor in glittering sheets, followed by smaller fragments that rattled down like hail. Cold air swept through the lobby, carrying exhaust, cordite, and the distant wail of approaching sirens.

Eli had almost reached the side corridor when a stray bullet caught him in the shoulder.

At first, he thought someone had shoved him from behind. His upper body twisted, his feet tangled, and he went down hard among the glass. There was no pain—only a deep, stunning numbness and the strange sensation that his left arm no longer belonged to him. Then the pain arrived, hot and enormous, and he couldn’t get a full breath.

He tried to push himself up. His arm folded uselessly beneath him.

Blood spread darkly through his shirt as he dragged himself behind the deposit counter. Around him, the crossfire hammered on: muzzle flashes, splintering wood, glass popping under boots. Eli pressed his back to the cabinet and stared at a shard of window beside his hand, watching his own reflection shiver each time another shot shook the building.

A bare room. On the table between them: a clock, a pencil, and a glass of water. The captive’s wrists are bound. The torturer has not raised their voice.

**TORTURER:** The password.

**CAPTIVE:** You’ve asked me that forty times.

**TORTURER:** Thirty-two. You’ve answered nine different ways. I found that encouraging.

**CAPTIVE:** I find you easy to encourage.

The torturer turns the clock so its face is visible to them both.

**TORTURER:** At twelve, I am going to hurt you.

**CAPTIVE:** You’ve been trying to scare me all night.

**TORTURER:** No. I’ve been waiting for you to do that yourself.

**CAPTIVE:** And if I’m not scared?

**TORTURER:** Then you won’t mind the wait.

The captive glances at the clock. Eleven fifty-three.

**CAPTIVE:** What happens at twelve?

**TORTURER:** Don’t ask how. You’ve been asking all evening, in one way or another. You want a shape for it. Something you can picture, something you can rehearse enduring.

**CAPTIVE:** You talk too much.

**TORTURER:** And you swallow every time I stop.

The captive says nothing. The ticking seems to deepen.

**TORTURER:** Drink some water.

**CAPTIVE:** No.

**TORTURER:** Your mouth is dry.

**CAPTIVE:** I said no.

**TORTURER:** As you like. Thirst gives fear something to impersonate. It can be difficult to tell them apart.

**CAPTIVE:** Is that what this is? A lesson?

**TORTURER:** A clarification. At present, you still believe there are two possibilities: that you give me the password, or that you don’t. By twelve, you’ll understand there are three.

**CAPTIVE:** What’s the third?

**TORTURER:** That you spend the rest of your life wondering whether you would have given it to me at twelve-oh-one.

The captive’s jaw tightens.

**CAPTIVE:** If I tell you, people die.

**TORTURER:** Yes.

**CAPTIVE:** That’s all you have to say?

**TORTURER:** Would you prefer me to argue? To tell you they’re enemies, or strangers, or already dead? They matter to you. That is why you’re suffering. I won’t insult you by pretending otherwise.

**CAPTIVE:** I’m not suffering.

**TORTURER:** Not yet. That’s the obscenity of anticipation, isn’t it? Nothing has happened, and still some part of you is begging.

**CAPTIVE:** You enjoy this.

**TORTURER:** You need me to. If I enjoy it, I’m a monster, and monsters can be hated. If I don’t, I’m simply waiting—and you have to wait with me.

The captive looks toward the door.

**TORTURER:** No one is coming through it.

**CAPTIVE:** You don’t know that.

**TORTURER:** No. But you looked anyway.

Eleven fifty-seven. The torturer picks up the pencil, examines its point, and sets it down again.

**CAPTIVE:** You’re afraid I don’t know it.

For the first time, the torturer hesitates.

**CAPTIVE:** There. You have a clock too.

**TORTURER:** Yes. But mine is on the table.

**CAPTIVE:** If you were certain, you wouldn’t still be talking.

**TORTURER:** I’m talking because silence would make you feel alone. I don’t want you alone yet.

The minute hand shudders forward.

**TORTURER:** One minute. Listen to how generous that sounds. One whole minute. Enough time to be brave. Enough time to imagine being brave afterward.

**CAPTIVE:** Go to hell.

**TORTURER:** You keep offering passwords to rooms I’m not trying to enter.

The captive stares at the glass of water. Their breathing quickens.

**TORTURER:** Not the water. The word.

**CAPTIVE:** And if I give it to you?

**TORTURER:** Then we put away the clock.

**CAPTIVE:** And I’m supposed to believe you?

**TORTURER:** No. But you’ll want to. Wanting to will be enough to begin.

The hand reaches twelve. Somewhere in the walls, a pipe knocks.

**CAPTIVE:** Wait.

**TORTURER:** I have.

The captive opens their mouth. Closes it.

The torturer pushes the pencil aside and slowly stands.

**TORTURER:** Very well. We’ll ask your silence instead.

The first breath was a mistake.

Smoke flooded Mara’s lungs, hot and thick enough to taste. Her chest seized. She tried to cough, but there was nothing clean to pull in afterward—only more smoke, scraping deeper, until she folded around the pain and saw white sparks at the edges of her vision.

*Get low. Get low.*

She dropped to her hands and knees. The floor scorched her palms.

Above her, the warehouse roared. Not crackled—roared, a vast, hungry sound that swallowed her screams. Beams groaned overhead. Somewhere behind her, glass burst with a flat, vicious bang.

This was no accident. The loading door had been chained from the outside. And twenty minutes ago, Lucian Vale had stood across the street, watching her walk inside.

Mara crawled.

Her thoughts broke apart into bright, useless fragments.

*Window. Too high. Phone. Upstairs. Door. Chained. Breathe. Don’t breathe. Don’t—*

Another breath convulsed through her before she could stop it. She gagged, pressing her mouth into the crook of her elbow. Her eyes streamed so hard she could barely see. Every few seconds, she lifted her head and shouted for help, but each shout came out smaller than the last.

The heat found her left arm.

At first it felt like a tight band around her wrist. Then her sleeve began to smolder. She slapped at it frantically, whimpering when the fabric stuck to her skin. Beneath it, angry blisters had already risen along her forearm.

Panic finally tore loose of thought.

She scrambled forward, careless now, slamming her shoulder into a crate, changing direction, striking another. The building had become a maze designed to forget her. Her lungs pumped uselessly. Her heartbeat battered her ribs. All she could think was that Lucian was outside somewhere, perhaps listening, perhaps waiting for the noise inside her to stop.

Then her hand struck empty space.

A doorway.

Cooler air—barely, but enough—slid across her face. Mara sobbed and dragged herself toward it. Through the smoke, she saw the pale rectangle of an open door and, beyond it, the night.

Almost.

A hand shot out of the darkness and closed around her blistered wrist.

She screamed, then clutched it anyway, relief flooding her so violently that her whole body shook.

Someone had come.

Then her fingers brushed metal: a heavy signet ring, its surface carved into the shape of a wolf’s head.

Lucian’s ring.

Mara looked up.

“Not yet,” he said, and began to pull her back into the smoke.

The rain had been working on the city all night. It hadn’t made a dent.

I put the case on the bed and opened it. No ceremony. Ceremony is for weddings and funerals, and nobody hires me for either until it’s too late.

A towel on the dresser, so nothing would knock. Lamp turned away, so my hands could work without showing the window what they knew. Then the pieces, one at a time. I looked each over without really seeing it. Seeing is for admirers. I was looking for flaws.

Fit. Seat. Tighten. Check.

I brought the main parts together, settled the assembly into its frame, and fixed the glass in place. Slow hands. No affection. I ran a finger along the seams, tested the few things that were supposed to move and the many that weren’t, then started over when one small doubt tapped me on the shoulder.

Doubt gets one rehearsal. After that, it’s stage fright.

The file said my target was a monster. Files are written by people who need monsters. Maybe he was. He’d signed papers, and afterward men had gone into the ground with their names spelled wrong. That ought to have made it simple.

It didn’t.

The man paying me had clean fingernails and a moral explanation. I’ve learned to trust clean fingernails about as far as I can throw the hand attached to them. His money was good, though. Money always is. That’s the nicest thing about it and the worst.

I finished the assembly and set the rifle down without loading it. There’s a religion in that pause, if you’re desperate enough to look for one. Metal on one side. Consequence on the other. Me in the middle, pretending I was only the bridge.

People think conscience arrives like a cop, all lights and shouting. Mine came like a room-service waiter: polite, intermittent, easy to tip and forget. It asked whether killing a bad man made me good, or just useful. Whether a person could do this enough times and still call the leftover thing a soul.

I didn’t have answers. Answers are heavy, and I travel light.

Across the avenue, a window went yellow. A figure crossed it and became a man for half a second. That was careless of him. Better for both of us if he’d stayed an address.

I made the last check. Everything was where I’d put it. Nothing rattled. Nothing forgave me.

“All right,” I said.

Not to him. Not to God. To the fellow in the mirror who’d been waiting all night to see which one of us was going to blink.

Then I picked up the rifle, and let him watch.

I ran a finger along the seams, tested the few things that were supposed to move and the many that weren’t, then started over when one small doubt tapped me on the shoulder.

Doubt gets one rehearsal. After that, it’s stage fright.

The file said my target was a monster. Files are written by people who need monsters. Maybe he was. He’d signed papers, and afterward men had gone into the ground with their names spelled wrong. That ought to have made it simple.

It didn’t.

The man paying me had clean fingernails and a moral explanation. I’ve learned to trust clean fingernails about as far as I can throw the hand attached to them. His money was good, though. Money always is. That’s the nicest thing about it and the worst.

I finished the assembly and set the rifle down without loading it. There’s a religion in that pause, if you’re desperate enough to look for one. Metal on one side. Consequence on the other. Me in the middle, pretending I was only the bridge.

People think conscience arrives like a cop, all lights and shouting. Mine came like a room-service waiter: polite, intermittent, easy to tip and forget. It asked whether killing a bad man made me good, or just useful. Whether a person could do this enough times and still call the leftover thing a soul.

I didn’t have answers. Answers are heavy, and I travel light.

Across the avenue, a window went yellow. A figure crossed it and became a man for half a second. That was careless of him. Better for both of us if he’d stayed an address.

I made the last check. Everything was where I’d put it. Nothing rattled. Nothing forgave me.

“All right,” I said.

Not to him. Not to God. To the fellow in the mirror who’d been waiting all night to see which one of us was going to blink.

Then I picked up the rifle, and let him watch.

The envelope was too light. That was what ruined it.

Rain had stopped an hour earlier, but water still ticked from the fire escapes into the alley behind the Granada. Marek stood with his back to the bricks, a velvet bag of stolen rings in one hand and six hundred dollars in the other.

“We agreed on two thousand,” he said.

Soll’s eyes kept sliding toward the mouth of the alley. “Times are hard.”

Marek had until sunrise to pay what he owed. Soll had until sunrise to deliver what he’d promised. Neither could afford to walk away, which made walking away the only thing either of them could think about.

“You never had the rest,” Marek said.

Soll’s jaw tightened. “Give me the bag.”

Marek laughed, a short, ugly sound. “No.”

The knife came out of Soll’s coat. It was a narrow, cheap-looking thing, and his hand was shaking so badly that the blade caught the alley light in nervous little flashes.

“I can’t go back empty-handed,” he said.

For a moment, neither man moved. Then Soll stepped forward, and Marek caught his wrist.

There was no skill in what followed. They collided shoulder to shoulder, swearing into each other’s faces, shoes skidding on wet grit. Soll tried to wrench free; Marek held on because letting go seemed worse. They struck the dumpster hard enough to boom its hollow side. The envelope fell. A gust turned it over once and pinned it beneath Soll’s heel.

Marek’s foot slipped.

They went down sideways, tangled together. Something struck his flank—not a blow, exactly, but a deep, sudden pressure, followed by a small and terrible give.

Soll went still.

Then he was scrambling backward, staring. The knife clattered somewhere in the dark. He snatched the velvet bag from the ground and ran, his footsteps quick and uneven until the alley swallowed them.

Marek remained sitting against the dumpster.

For one strange second, there was almost no pain. Only cold at a single point high in his side, and an invasive fullness, as though something had been pressed deep into a place that had no room for it. He felt offended more than hurt. His body seemed to be waiting for an explanation.

Then the explanation arrived.

Heat spread around the cold. The pressure became a dense, grinding burn, and his shirt grew warm and heavy against his skin. When he tried to breathe, the breath stopped halfway. It felt as if a wire had been tightened around his ribs. Each careful inhalation woke a sharper pain beneath the first, bright enough to bleach the alley from his vision.

He pressed a hand to his side. His fingers came away slick, but looking at them made the strength drain from his arms, so he put the hand back.

His heartbeat had changed. He could feel it everywhere—in his throat, in his teeth, in the wound itself, where every pulse seemed to knock from the inside. His legs had become distant, unreliable things. The alley smelled suddenly stronger: wet stone, rot, diesel, the iron tang rising beneath it all.

A window opened above him. Marek tipped his head back but could not make his voice into anything larger than a rasp.

Far away, a siren started, faded, then started again.

He fixed his attention on the sound and took another shallow breath. It hurt. He took it anyway.

Rain ticked on the dumpster lid with the patience of a metronome. It carried the alley’s smells to Detective Mara Voss in layers: wet brick, rust, the vinegar reek of old urine, grease gone rancid behind the restaurant. Beneath it all was something lower and warmer—copper, and the heavy, sweet stink of an opened body.

Voss snapped on a pair of nitrile gloves and ducked beneath the tape.

The dead man sat with his shoulders against the wall and his legs folded badly beneath him. His overcoat had been buttoned after the killing. Whoever did it had taken care with the buttons, though not with him. Rain had washed his face clean except where blood remained trapped in the seams of his mouth. Each drop from the fire escape struck his forehead and made his eyelids tremble. Nothing else in him moved.

A uniformed officer named Pell stood nearby, holding a flashlight at an unhelpful angle.

“Jesus,” he said quietly.

Voss looked up. “Your log says you arrived at three twelve.”

“Yes.”

“Then you’ve had twenty minutes for that. Bring the light here.”

He brought it.

She crouched. Cold water soaked instantly through the knee of her trousers. Her hands remained steady as she opened the dead man’s coat.

The shirt beneath had been cut from breastbone to belly. The fabric was black and rigid with blood, but rain had bleached the wound’s outer edges to a greyish pink. A loop of intestine rested against his thigh, blue-grey and glistening. When Voss lifted the shirt, wet cloth adhered to the torn flesh, then came free with a soft, intimate sound.

Pell’s flashlight wavered.

“Hold it still.”

She examined the body in the order she always did: hands, shoes, pockets, face. Wounds last. Wounds encouraged people to imagine; the rest of the body was more likely to answer questions.

There were no cuts across the palms. The right thumbnail was torn down to the quick, and something dark had dried beneath the remaining nails. A pale band circled the fourth finger of his left hand where a ring had recently been. His shoes were expensive leather, ruined by the alley water, but the treads were clean. No grit. No mud. No blood pressed into the seams.

No wallet in the trousers. No phone in the coat. Voss noted both absences without naming them robbery.

She pressed two fingers against the discoloration at his jaw. It did not blanch. Through the glove, his skin felt dense and cold. The medical examiner would offer an estimate polished with qualifications. Voss needed only a place to begin.

Behind the body, blood had run along the uneven concrete and gathered at a clogged drain, where it trembled beneath the rain, black and skinned with oil. The brick above it was nearly clean. No high spray. No scattered drops. No frantic handprints.

Nothing here had happened the way the body wanted it to look.

Voss angled the light toward the left shoe. A pale curl was wedged into the welt, so small she almost mistook it for a flake of paint. She removed it with tweezers and held it beneath the beam.

Wood. Freshly cut, by the look of it.

She opened an evidence bag. The rain found the inside of her collar and ran down her spine.

“What is it?” Pell asked.

“Something that isn’t from this alley.”

She sealed the bag and wrote the time across it in a small, level hand: **03:47**.

Around them, the city continued at its usual volume. A truck changed gears on the avenue. Bottles rattled in a recycling bin. Somewhere above the alley, a window shut.

Voss stood, feeling the stiffness in her knee and the wet cloth clamped to it. She gave the dead man’s face one final look, not from pity and not from curiosity, but because the face belonged in the record too.

“Get the photographer back in here,” she said. “Then we move him.”

The rain went on thinning the blood, carrying it patiently toward the drain. By morning, the alley would smell of rust and garbage again.

Voss intended to have the truth written down before then.

The heat pressed against her before the flames did, tightening her skin until it felt a size too small. Then the pain sharpened—an intimate, crawling agony that spread across her arms and neck. Blisters rose in taut, shining welts, each one exquisitely sensitive. When her sleeve shifted, the fabric dragged over them, and she cried out, only to suck smoke into her mouth.

She tried to hold her breath. Her body wouldn’t let her.

A shallow gasp brought heat instead of air. Her throat clenched; her chest heaved uselessly, dragging in another scorching mouthful. Coughing bent her double, but even between coughs she couldn’t find enough oxygen. The room pulsed orange around her. Somewhere beyond it was the door—she was almost certain—but her thoughts had narrowed to a single animal command: *breathe*.

She clawed at her collar, then at the floor, panic convincing her that air might be hiding somewhere close, somewhere just out of reach. Her lungs burned with the effort of expanding. Black spots gathered at the edges of her vision, swelling and shrinking with her heartbeat. For one terrible second, she forgot why she was crawling. She only knew that she had to keep moving, because stopping meant surrendering to the next breath—and the next breath might not come.
